title: The Mirror-Image Test for an Opioid Receptor — Goldstein's Stereospecificity, Pert & Snyder's [3H]Naloxone Levorphanol vs. Dextrorphan Assay & Enkephalin Discovery

teenKit.tldr: Scientists used to know drugs like painkillers worked in the brain without any way to see the actual machinery doing it. By using radioactive tags and left-versus-right mirror-image molecules, researchers finally proved physical opioid receptors actually exist.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how chemicals lock into microscopic brain receptors is the foundation of modern pharmacology, driving how we design safer medicines and understand addiction.
keyTakeaways: Before high-tech microscopes could image proteins, scientists had to use clever logic and radioactive detective work to prove receptors existed.
The mirror-image test (enantiomers) proved receptors are picky shapes because a drug's left-handed version worked while its exact right-handed twin did nothing.
Discovering that our brains make their own natural painkillers (enkephalins) proved that drugs were just hijacking an already existing cellular messaging system.

vocab.meaning: The biological rule that a receptor only fits a molecule with a very specific three-dimensional shape, much like a custom lock and key.
One of a pair of molecules that are exact mirror images of each other, yet often behave totally differently in biology.
An experimental technique using a radioactive tag attached to a chemical to track exactly where and how it binds to cells.
A naturally occurring peptide made inside your own body that binds to opioid receptors to manage pain and stress.

quiz.question: Why couldn't scientists just use a standard microscope to find opioid receptors when they first suspected they existed?
options: Microscopes weren't invented yet in the 1970s.
Receptors are vastly outnumbered by other proteins and far too small to see directly.
Receptors only exist when a person is actively experiencing pain.
Light passes right through biological tissues without hitting cells.
quiz.explanation: Receptors are microscopic proteins deeply embedded in cell membranes, making them completely invisible to standard imaging tools.

quiz.question: What was the brilliant logic behind using mirror-image molecules (enantiomers) like levorphanol and dextrorphan?
options: One mirror image would glow in the dark while the other would stay black.
If a biological receptor was real, it would only fit one specific mirror-image shape, proving the effect wasn't just random chance.
It was the only chemical combination that didn't destroy the pig brains used in the lab.
Mirror-image molecules are naturally radioactive without needing a lab to alter them.
quiz.explanation: Because biological targets have precise shapes, only the correct stereoisomer will fit into the receptor lock.

quiz.question: What did the discovery of enkephalins by Hughes and colleagues tell us about the brain?
options: That the human brain actually manufactures its own natural versions of opioid painkillers.
That external drugs like morphine are chemically identical to plant roots.
That pig brains operate on completely different rules than human brains.
That brain receptors can change their shape whenever they encounter radiation.
quiz.explanation: Finding enkephalins proved that plant-derived opioids were effective only because they mimicked chemicals our bodies already make.
